title: Women's voices today
hookLine: women serve as granthis and ragis, and Sikhs discuss where women may do kirtan

lines: A WOMAN AT THE GURU'S SIDE.
cards: Why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? That question is Guru Nanak's, in the Guru Granth Sahib. Hold it in mind.

An ordinary evening in a gurdwara. A woman sits behind the Guru Granth Sahib, reading aloud, waving the chaur over the open pages. Later, a group of women sit at the harmonium and sing the evening hymns.
In this hall, it's ordinary. And yet, in some places, Sikhs are still discussing where women's kirtan groups may sing. Today: a teaching that is clear, and a conversation that isn't finished.

teach.b: At Ang 473 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn of Guru Nanak, the Guru says that we are born of woman, we marry woman, through woman friendships and families are made, and then he asks: why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?
The question is the teaching. Second, the practice today.
Sikh women serve as granthis, reading from and caring for the Guru Granth Sahib, and as ragis, singing kirtan.
Women serve on gurdwara committees, cook and serve langar, and take part in the Panj Pyare in some congregations, while others keep that role for men.
The Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, opens the main parts of gurdwara life to Sikh men and women alike. Third, the open question.
At Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the kirtan in the inner sanctum has traditionally been sung by men's groups, and some Sikhs have asked that women's groups sing there too.
Some point to Ang 473 and say the Gurus' teaching on equality already settles it. Others say a change at that place should come through the Panth's own institutions, in their own time.
The question has been raised more than once, and it is still being discussed. Fourth, the shape of it.
The teaching is clear, and the practice is wide; one place, and some roles, are still under discussion.
It's honest to say it's open, and honest to say whose words both sides are reaching for.

how: In gurdwaras, Sikh women read from the Guru Granth Sahib, sing kirtan, serve langar and sit on committees; the question of women's kirtan groups in the inner sanctum of Harmandir Sahib is still discussed within the Panth.

games.q: someone in the langar hall says women's voices count for less in the Guru's house. which answer comes from the Guru Granth Sahib?
o: why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?
women may sing, but only at home.
games.why: Guru Nanak's question at Ang 473 is the Guru's own answer.

practice: Think of a conversation in your own life that isn't finished yet, in your family, your work, your community, and don't try to win it now.

Breathe in and hear the strongest point on one side; breathe out and hear the strongest point on the other, noticing where you lean and what you might still be missing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
